facts.raw_span: A 60-year-old Saudi man presented with an 18-month history of erythroderma affecting his entire body and face
slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area
confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles
sparing of the nails and scalp
Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present
no palpable lymphadenopathy
epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis
Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG
Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7
CD30 was positive in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes

concepts.why: The patient's presentation of erythroderma, lichenified erythromelanotic plaques, and atypical lymphocytes with epidermotropism is consistent with Mycosis Fungoides, a type of Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma.

support_spans: A 60-year-old Saudi man presented with an 18-month history of erythroderma affecting his entire body and face
confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles
epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis
concepts.why: The patient's presentation of erythroderma and atypical lymphocytes with epidermotropism is consistent with Sézary Syndrome, a leukemic form of Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma, although the absence of lymphadenopathy is not typical.
It explains the presence of bilateral lower-lid ectropion and the specific immunohistochemical staining pattern of the tumor cells.

rationales.F02: Pruritic lesions are common in both Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome, but slightly more characteristic of the former.
rationales.F03: Confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques are more typical of Mycosis Fungoides, but can also be seen in Sézary Syndrome.
rationales.F04: Sparing of the nails and scalp is less common in Sézary Syndrome, which often presents with more widespread involvement.
rationales.F05: Bilateral lower-lid ectropion can be seen in both conditions, but is slightly more common in Sézary Syndrome.
rationales.F07: Epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes is a hallmark of Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome, strongly supporting both diagnoses.
rationales.F09: Immunohistochemical staining showing tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7 is highly suggestive of both Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome.
rationales.F10: CD30 positivity in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes may be seen in both conditions, but is slightly more characteristic of Sézary Syndrome.

frontier_selector.why: The presence of epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes and specific immunohistochemical staining patterns, such as tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7, decided it.
